claim: Sepsis mortality rates remain high, with up to 50%.
source: In spite of the successful use of antimicrobial therapies, mortality rates remain high, with up to 50% (Mayr et al., 2014; Holzheimer et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayr et al., 2014 and Holzheimer et al., 1991

claim: The main determinant of sepsis-associated mortality is the combination of dysregulated systemic inflammation, immune paralysis, and hemostatic abnormalities that together cause multiorgan failure.
source: The main determinant of sepsis-associated mortality is rarely the pathogen, but instead the combination of dysregulated systemic inflammation, immune paralysis, and hemostatic abnormalities that together cause multiorgan failure (Singer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singer et al., 2016

claim: Upon pathogen sensing, inflammation promotes the activation of coagulation, which generates factors that further amplify inflammation, creating a self-amplifying cycle.
source: Upon pathogen sensing, ensuing inflammation promotes the activation of coagulation, which in turn generates factors that further amplify inflammation, thus creating a vicious, self-amplifying cycle.
evidence: Supported by citations to Semeraro et al., 2015 and Gando et al., 2016 in the following sentence

claim: Systemic inflammation and widespread formation of microvascular thrombi together cause vascular leak, occlusion of small vessels, and eventually multiorgan failure.
source: These events result in systemic inflammation and the widespread formation of microvascular thrombi, that together cause vascular leak, occlusion of small vessels, and eventually multiorgan failure (Semeraro et al., 2015; Gando et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Semeraro et al., 2015 and Gando et al., 2016

claim: Sepsis is accompanied by immune cell dysfunction characterized by immune cell exhaustion, enhanced apoptosis and impaired antigen presentation, cytokine production, and pathogen killing.
source: At the same time, sepsis goes along with a state of immune cell dysfunction characterized by immune cell exhaustion, enhanced apoptosis and impaired antigen presentation, cytokine production, and pathogen killing (Hotchkiss et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hotchkiss et al., 2013

claim: LPS is an important driver of inflammation during Gram-negative sepsis due to its ability to activate TLR-4.
source: The potent immunogen lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is an important driver of inflammation during Gram-negative sepsis, due to its ability to activate toll-like receptor (TLR)–4 (Beutler, 2000; Hoshino et al., 1999) and caspase-11 (Hagar et al., 2013; Kayagaki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beutler, 2000 and Hoshino et al., 1999

claim: LPS is an important driver of inflammation during Gram-negative sepsis due to its ability to activate caspase-11.
source: The potent immunogen lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is an important driver of inflammation during Gram-negative sepsis, due to its ability to activate toll-like receptor (TLR)–4 (Beutler, 2000; Hoshino et al., 1999) and caspase-11 (Hagar et al., 2013; Kayagaki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hagar et al., 2013 and Kayagaki et al., 2013

claim: LPS-tolerance is characterized by an unresponsive state of myeloid cells after repeated TLR stimulation.
source: The state of sepsis-induced immune paralysis can be partially recapitulated in vitro by the phenomenon of LPS-tolerance, which is characterized by an unresponsive state of myeloid cells after repeated TLR stimulation (de Vos et al., 2009; Fan and Cook, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Vos et al., 2009 and Fan and Cook, 2004

claim: Disease tolerance describes a host defense strategy that minimizes the detrimental impact of infection irrespective of the pathogen burden.
source: In contrast, the concept of 'disease tolerance' describes a poorly studied, yet essential host defense strategy, on top of the well understood strategies of avoidance and resistance (Medzhitov et al., 2012). While avoidance means preventing pathogen exposure and infection, and resistance aims to more efficiently reduce the pathogen load in the course of an established infection, disease tolerance involves mechanisms, which minimize the detrimental impact of infection irrespective of the pathogen burden, thus improving host fitness despite the infection for example by improving tissue damage control (Medzhitov et al., 2012; Martins et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Medzhitov et al., 2012 and Martins et al., 2019

claim: LPS pretreatment 24 hr prior to infection significantly improved pathogen clearance.
source: While LPS pretreatment 24 hr prior to infection significantly improved pathogen clearance, any longer period (i.e. 2–8 weeks) between LPS administration and infection did not affect the bacterial load when compared to control mice (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: LPS pretreatment 2-8 weeks prior to infection did not affect the bacterial load when compared to control mice.
source: While LPS pretreatment 24 hr prior to infection significantly improved pathogen clearance, any longer period (i.e. 2–8 weeks) between LPS administration and infection did not affect the bacterial load when compared to control mice (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: All LPS pretreated groups (1 day to 8 weeks) were substantially protected from sepsis-associated tissue damage, illustrated by the absence of elevated liver transaminase plasma levels.
source: Importantly, though all LPS pretreated groups were substantially protected from sepsis-associated tissue damage, illustrated by the absence of elevated liver transaminase (aspartate aminotransferase [ASAT] and alanine aminotransferase [ALAT]) plasma levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Short-term (24 hr) LPS pre-exposure improved resistance to infection and consequently tissue integrity.
source: Thus, short-term (24 hr) LPS pre-exposure improved resistance to infection and consequently tissue integrity, while long-term (2–8 weeks) LPS pre-exposure enabled the maintenance of tissue integrity irrespective of a high bacterial load, which per definition resembles disease tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing improved pathogen clearance and reduced tissue damage at 24 hr

claim: Long-term (2-8 weeks) LPS pre-exposure enabled the maintenance of tissue integrity irrespective of a high bacterial load, which resembles disease tolerance.
source: Thus, short-term (24 hr) LPS pre-exposure improved resistance to infection and consequently tissue integrity, while long-term (2–8 weeks) LPS pre-exposure enabled the maintenance of tissue integrity irrespective of a high bacterial load, which per definition resembles disease tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing maintained tissue integrity despite high bacterial load at 2-8 weeks

claim: Organ protection in tolerant mice was associated with the absence of liver necrosis.
source: Doing so, we observed that organ protection (Figure 1B) was associated with the absence of liver necrosis (Figure 1D and E), while inflammatory cytokine and chemokine levels were indistinguishable between sensitive and tolerant mice 18 hr post-infection (p.i.) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: Inflammatory cytokine and chemokine levels were indistinguishable between sensitive and tolerant mice 18 hr post-infection.
source: Doing so, we observed that organ protection (Figure 1B) was associated with the absence of liver necrosis (Figure 1D and E), while inflammatory cytokine and chemokine levels were indistinguishable between sensitive and tolerant mice 18 hr post-infection (p.i.) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: Tolerant mice maintained significantly higher blood platelet counts upon E. coli infection compared to sensitive mice.
source: While we discovered a severe decline in platelet numbers upon E. coli infection in sensitive mice, tolerant mice maintained significantly higher blood platelet counts (Figure 1G) and, in sharp contrast to sensitive animals, showed almost no deposition of micro-thrombi in liver (Figure 1H and I) and lung sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that tissue damage control occurred systemic and not organ specific.
evidence: Supported by platelet count data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Tolerant mice showed almost no deposition of micro-thrombi in liver and lung sections.
source: While we discovered a severe decline in platelet numbers upon E. coli infection in sensitive mice, tolerant mice maintained significantly higher blood platelet counts (Figure 1G) and, in sharp contrast to sensitive animals, showed almost no deposition of micro-thrombi in liver (Figure 1H and I) and lung sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that tissue damage control occurred systemic and not organ specific.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1H, I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Tissue damage control in tolerant mice occurred systemically and not organ specific.
source: While we discovered a severe decline in platelet numbers upon E. coli infection in sensitive mice, tolerant mice maintained significantly higher blood platelet counts (Figure 1G) and, in sharp contrast to sensitive animals, showed almost no deposition of micro-thrombi in liver (Figure 1H and I) and lung sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that tissue damage control occurred systemic and not organ specific.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced micro-thrombi in multiple organs (liver and lung)

claim: Sensitive and tolerant mice showed similar platelet counts at the onset of E. coli infection (2 weeks post-LPS).
source: Considering that LPS exposure itself can impact coagulation factor levels and blood platelet numbers (Asakura et al., 2003; Ohtaki et al., 2002), we importantly found similar platelet counts in sensitive and tolerant mice at the onset of E. coli infection (2 weeks post-LPS) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by platelet count data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Sensitive and tolerant mice showed similar plasma thrombin generation potential prior to infection.
source: In addition, we did not detect any indication for an altered coagulation potential in tolerant mice before sepsis induction, as both groups showed a similar plasma thrombin generation potential prior to infection (Figure 1J left panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by thrombin generation assay data shown in Figure 1J left panel and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: The thrombin generation capacity was preserved in tolerant mice after infection (18 hr p.i.) compared to sensitive animals.
source: However, compared to sensitive animals, the thrombin generation capacity was only preserved in tolerant mice after infection (18 hr p.i.), suggesting that tolerance mechanisms prevented sepsis-associated consumption coagulopathy (Figure 1J right panel and 1 K).
evidence: Supported by thrombin generation assay data shown in Figure 1J right panel and 1K

claim: Tolerance mechanisms prevented sepsis-associated consumption coagulopathy.
source: However, compared to sensitive animals, the thrombin generation capacity was only preserved in tolerant mice after infection (18 hr p.i.), suggesting that tolerance mechanisms prevented sepsis-associated consumption coagulopathy (Figure 1J right panel and 1 K).
evidence: Inferred from the preserved thrombin generation capacity in tolerant mice

claim: The absence of lymphocytes in Rag2-/- animals resulted in profoundly reduced liver damage upon bacterial infection of naïve, sensitive mice.
source: Strikingly, the absence of lymphocytes, as in Rag2 deficient (Rag2-/-) animals, already resulted in profoundly reduced liver damage upon bacterial infection of naïve, sensitive mice and fully abrogated further LPS-induced tissue protection without affecting the bacterial load (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The absence of lymphocytes in Rag2-/- animals fully abrogated LPS-induced tissue protection without affecting the bacterial load.
source: Strikingly, the absence of lymphocytes, as in Rag2 deficient (Rag2-/-) animals, already resulted in profoundly reduced liver damage upon bacterial infection of naïve, sensitive mice and fully abrogated further LPS-induced tissue protection without affecting the bacterial load (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase and bacterial load data shown in Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Lymphocytes contribute to the sensitivity of animals to sepsis-associated organ damage in naïve mice.
source: This indicated that lymphocytes on the one hand importantly contributed to the sensitivity of animals to sepsis-associated organ damage in naïve mice, and on the other hand were essential in mediating LPS-induced tissue protection in tolerant hosts.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced liver damage in lymphocyte-deficient Rag2-/- mice

claim: Lymphocytes are essential in mediating LPS-induced tissue protection in tolerant hosts.
source: This indicated that lymphocytes on the one hand importantly contributed to the sensitivity of animals to sepsis-associated organ damage in naïve mice, and on the other hand were essential in mediating LPS-induced tissue protection in tolerant hosts.
evidence: Inferred from the abrogation of LPS-induced protection in lymphocyte-deficient Rag2-/- mice

claim: Adoptive transfer of splenocytes into Rag2-/- mice re-established LPS-induced tissue damage control.
source: In support of this, adoptive transfer of splenocytes into Rag2-/- mice re-established LPS-induced tissue damage control (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Depleting CD8 or CD4 T cells prior to LPS exposure neither affected the difference between sensitive and tolerant animals to organ damage nor the bacterial load upon E. coli infection.
source: Depleting CD8 or CD4 T cells, respectively, prior to LPS exposure (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) neither affected the difference between sensitive and tolerant animals to organ damage (Figure 2C) nor the bacterial load (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) upon E. coli infection.
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase and bacterial load data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: B cell deficiency (JHT mice) fully prevented the development of tissue damage during sepsis irrespective of tolerance induction.
source: In contrast, B cell deficiency (JHT mice) fully prevented the development of tissue damage during sepsis irrespective of tolerance induction (Figure 2D) and despite a high bacterial load (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2D

claim: B cell deficiency (JHT mice) prevented tissue damage during sepsis despite a high bacterial load.
source: In contrast, B cell deficiency (JHT mice) fully prevented the development of tissue damage during sepsis irrespective of tolerance induction (Figure 2D) and despite a high bacterial load (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: Adoptive transfer of B cells into Rag2-/- mice aggravated liver damage upon E. coli infection in sensitive mice.
source: Furthermore, adoptive transfer of B cells into Rag2-/- mice (Figure 2E) aggravated liver damage upon E. coli infection in sensitive and reestablished tissue protection in tolerant mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Adoptive transfer of B cells into Rag2-/- mice reestablished tissue protection in tolerant mice.
source: Furthermore, adoptive transfer of B cells into Rag2-/- mice (Figure 2E) aggravated liver damage upon E. coli infection in sensitive and reestablished tissue protection in tolerant mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2F

claim: B cells are involved in both sepsis-associated organ damage and the establishment of LPS-triggered disease tolerance.
source: These findings indicated that B cells, but not T cells, played an ambiguous role as they were involved in both, sepsis-associated organ damage and the establishment of LPS-triggered disease tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the B cell depletion and transfer experiments showing both damaging and protective effects

claim: Splenectomy was associated with reduced liver damage in naïve, sensitive mice.
source: We then tested if splenectomy would replicate the protective effects of full B cell deficiency during sepsis and interestingly found that splenectomy was associated with reduced liver damage in naïve, sensitive mice, which is in line with other studies (Agarwal et al., 1972; Karanfilian et al., 1983), but, in contrast to complete lymphocyte deficiency, not sufficient to abrogate LPS-induced tissue protection in tolerant animals (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2G and citations to Agarwal et al., 1972 and Karanfilian et al., 1983

claim: Splenectomy was not sufficient to abrogate LPS-induced tissue protection in tolerant animals.
source: We then tested if splenectomy would replicate the protective effects of full B cell deficiency during sepsis and interestingly found that splenectomy was associated with reduced liver damage in naïve, sensitive mice, which is in line with other studies (Agarwal et al., 1972; Karanfilian et al., 1983), but, in contrast to complete lymphocyte deficiency, not sufficient to abrogate LPS-induced tissue protection in tolerant animals (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: Mature splenic B cells contribute to tissue damage during severe infections.
source: This suggested that mature splenic B cells contributed to tissue damage during severe infections, while other, not spleen derived, B cell compartments were instrumental in driving disease tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the splenectomy experiments showing reduced damage in sensitive mice

claim: Non-spleen derived B cell compartments are instrumental in driving disease tolerance.
source: This suggested that mature splenic B cells contributed to tissue damage during severe infections, while other, not spleen derived, B cell compartments were instrumental in driving disease tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the splenectomy experiments showing maintained tolerance despite splenectomy

claim: Monocyte and macrophage depletion neither influenced sepsis-induced tissue damage in sensitive animals nor impacted LPS-induced tissue damage control.
source: Surprisingly, monocyte and macrophage depletion neither influenced sepsis-induced tissue damage in sensitive animals nor did it impact on LPS-induced tissue damage control (Figure 4A), suggesting that classical LPS-tolerance is not the sole reason for protection.
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Classical LPS-tolerance is not the sole reason for protection in tolerant mice.
source: Surprisingly, monocyte and macrophage depletion neither influenced sepsis-induced tissue damage in sensitive animals nor did it impact on LPS-induced tissue damage control (Figure 4A), suggesting that classical LPS-tolerance is not the sole reason for protection.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of monocyte/macrophage depletion on tissue protection

claim: Platelet or neutrophil depletion exerted tissue protective effects in both sensitive and tolerant mice.
source: Platelet or neutrophil depletion, in contrast, already exerted tissue protective effects in both groups, illustrated by greatly reduced ASAT levels in sensitive and tolerant mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 4A

claim: LPS-pretreatment still enhanced tissue protection in platelet-depleted mice.
source: However, while LPS-pretreatment still enhanced tissue protection in ΔPlt mice, it did not result in any additive beneficial effects in ΔPMN animals (Figure 4A), similar to what we had observed upon B cell deficiency (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 4A

claim: LPS-pretreatment did not result in any additive beneficial effects in neutrophil-depleted animals.
source: However, while LPS-pretreatment still enhanced tissue protection in ΔPlt mice, it did not result in any additive beneficial effects in ΔPMN animals (Figure 4A), similar to what we had observed upon B cell deficiency (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Neutrophils are key effector cells of tissue protection in tolerant animals.
source: These data support the reported role of platelets and neutrophils in promoting tissue damage during sepsis (Semeraro et al., 2015; Gando et al., 2016) and proved neutrophils to be key effector cells of tissue protection in tolerant animals.
evidence: Inferred from the neutrophil depletion experiments showing abrogation of LPS-induced protection

claim: Tissue protection in tolerant mice was associated with elevated neutrophil abundance in blood and peritoneal lavage fluid.
source: While tissue protection was associated with elevated neutrophil abundance in blood and peritoneal lavage fluid (PLF) of septic wild type mice (Figure 4D and E), neutrophil extravasation into tissues such as the liver and lung were substantially reduced (Figure 4F–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and E

claim: Neutrophil extravasation into tissues such as the liver and lung were substantially reduced in tolerant mice.
source: While tissue protection was associated with elevated neutrophil abundance in blood and peritoneal lavage fluid (PLF) of septic wild type mice (Figure 4D and E), neutrophil extravasation into tissues such as the liver and lung were substantially reduced (Figure 4F–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4F-G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: In Rag2-/- and JHT mice, LPS pretreatment did not cause increased blood neutrophils nor a significant accumulation in the PLF during sepsis.
source: In both Rag2-/- and JHT mice, LPS pretreatment did not cause increased blood neutrophils nor a significant accumulation in the PLF during sepsis (Figure 4H–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G and H

claim: Infection-induced neutrophil migration into liver tissue was reduced after LPS pretreatment in JHT mice.
source: However, infection-induced neutrophil migration into liver tissue was still reduced after LPS pretreatment in JHT mice (Figure 4J), but not in Rag2-/- animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4J

claim: Infection-induced neutrophil migration into liver tissue was not reduced after LPS pretreatment in Rag2-/- animals.
source: However, infection-induced neutrophil migration into liver tissue was still reduced after LPS pretreatment in JHT mice (Figure 4J), but not in Rag2-/- animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I

claim: In tolerant animals, B cells affect systemic neutrophil trafficking and turnover after LPS-pre-exposure.
source: This suggested that in tolerant animals, B cells might affect systemic neutrophil trafficking and turnover after LPS-pre-exposure, whereas the suppressed neutrophil extravasation to the livers of tolerant mice occurred independent of B cells.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of B cell deficiency on neutrophil abundance in blood/PLF versus liver

claim: The suppressed neutrophil extravasation to the livers of tolerant mice occurred independent of B cells.
source: This suggested that in tolerant animals, B cells might affect systemic neutrophil trafficking and turnover after LPS-pre-exposure, whereas the suppressed neutrophil extravasation to the livers of tolerant mice occurred independent of B cells.
evidence: Inferred from the maintained reduction in liver neutrophils in JHT mice after LPS pretreatment

claim: Blood neutrophils of tolerant mice expressed lower CD62L levels upon infection than those of sensitive controls.
source: In support of this idea, we discovered that blood neutrophils of tolerant mice expressed lower CD62L levels upon infection than those of sensitive controls, and that this phenotype required the presence of B cells (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4K

claim: The lower CD62L expression on blood neutrophils of tolerant mice required the presence of B cells.
source: In support of this idea, we discovered that blood neutrophils of tolerant mice expressed lower CD62L levels upon infection than those of sensitive controls, and that this phenotype required the presence of B cells (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4K

claim: Decreased CD62L expression is indicative of neutrophil aging, a process that is counteracted by Cxcr4 signaling.
source: While CD62L has been studied extensively for its importance in neutrophil adhesion and rolling over the vascular endothelium (Ivetic, 2018), a recent study has identified decreased CD62L expression indicative of neutrophil aging, a process that is counteracted by Cxcr4 signaling, the master regulator of neutrophil trafficking between the bone marrow and the periphery (Adrover et al., 2019; Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adrover et al., 2019; Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003

claim: Cxcr4 is the master regulator of neutrophil trafficking between the bone marrow and the periphery.
source: While CD62L has been studied extensively for its importance in neutrophil adhesion and rolling over the vascular endothelium (Ivetic, 2018), a recent study has identified decreased CD62L expression indicative of neutrophil aging, a process that is counteracted by Cxcr4 signaling, the master regulator of neutrophil trafficking between the bone marrow and the periphery (Adrover et al., 2019; Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adrover et al., 2019; Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003

claim: Tolerant mice exhibited a sustained transcriptional reprogramming of the neutrophil pool.
source: Despite the supposedly short life span of neutrophils, tolerant mice exhibited a sustained transcriptional reprogramming of the neutrophil pool.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data showing differential gene expression

claim: Principal component analysis of the 1000 most variable genes revealed clustering of neutrophils according to the site of sampling.
source: Principal component analysis of the 1000 most variable genes revealed clustering of neutrophils according to the site of sampling (Figure 5A), likely reflecting the heterogeneity of neutrophils in bone marrow versus mature cells in blood (Semerad et al., 2002; Evrard et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Samples further separated according to treatment (LPS vs NaCl).
source: Samples further separated according to treatment (Figure 5A) and we identified a substantial number of tolerance associated, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in both, bone marrow and blood neutrophils (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C and D; Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5A

claim: A substantial number of tolerance associated, differentially expressed genes were identified in both bone marrow and blood neutrophils.
source: Samples further separated according to treatment (Figure 5A) and we identified a substantial number of tolerance associated, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in both, bone marrow and blood neutrophils (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C and D; Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C and D

claim: Blood neutrophil DEGs exhibited an enrichment of genes associated with immunity and defense responses.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of blood neutrophil DEGs exhibited an enrichment of genes associated with immunity and defense responses (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Bone marrow neutrophils of tolerant mice showed an enrichment of genes associated with cell migration, trafficking, and chemotaxis.
source: Strikingly, bone marrow neutrophils of tolerant mice showed an enrichment of genes associated with cell migration, trafficking, and chemotaxis (Figure 5C), such as genes involved in Cxcl12/Cxcr4 signaling including Cxcr4 itself (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Bone marrow neutrophils of tolerant mice showed enrichment of genes involved in Cxcl12/Cxcr4 signaling including Cxcr4 itself.
source: Strikingly, bone marrow neutrophils of tolerant mice showed an enrichment of genes associated with cell migration, trafficking, and chemotaxis (Figure 5C), such as genes involved in Cxcl12/Cxcr4 signaling including Cxcr4 itself (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: Cxcr4 expression was upregulated on bone marrow derived neutrophils of tolerant mice compared to sensitive control mice on a transcriptional level.
source: Considering the reported importance of Cxcr4 signaling in neutrophil retention in the bone marrow and their release to the periphery (Adrover et al., 2019; Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003), we verified an upregulation of Cxcr4 on bone marrow derived neutrophils of tolerant mice compared to sensitive control mice on a transcriptional (Figure 5D) and protein level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Cxcr4 expression was upregulated on bone marrow derived neutrophils of tolerant mice compared to sensitive control mice on a protein level.
source: Considering the reported importance of Cxcr4 signaling in neutrophil retention in the bone marrow and their release to the periphery (Adrover et al., 2019; Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003), we verified an upregulation of Cxcr4 on bone marrow derived neutrophils of tolerant mice compared to sensitive control mice on a transcriptional (Figure 5D) and protein level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F

claim: Cxcr4 induction on neutrophils depended on B cells, as Cxcr4 expression levels did not change in neutrophils isolated from LPS pre-exposed JHT mice.
source: Importantly, this Cxcr4 induction depended on B cells, as Cxcr4 expression levels did not change in neutrophils isolated from LPS pre-exposed JHT mice (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F

claim: Liver histology reflected the tissue protective effects of ATI2341 treatment, while control and ADM3100 treated mice developed profound liver necrosis.
source: Liver histology reflected the tissue protective effects of ATI2341 treatment, while control and ADM3100 treated mice developed profound liver necrosis (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5G

claim: None of the Cxcr4 treatments (ATI2341 or AMD3100) altered the bacterial load.
source: At the same time, none of these treatments altered the bacterial load (Figure 5H), suggesting that activation of Cxcr4 during sepsis induced disease tolerance.
evidence: Supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 5H

claim: Activation of Cxcr4 during sepsis induced disease tolerance.
source: At the same time, none of these treatments altered the bacterial load (Figure 5H), suggesting that activation of Cxcr4 during sepsis induced disease tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the tissue protection without affecting bacterial load

claim: B cells act as important regulators of granulopoiesis and neutrophil trafficking at steady state and under inflammatory conditions.
source: Based on our finding of a long-lasting transcriptional reprogramming in the neutrophil compartment and B cell dependency of tolerance-associated Cxcr4 upregulation, it is tempting to speculate that B cells act as important regulators of granulopoiesis and neutrophil trafficking at steady state and under inflammatory conditions.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the experimental findings

claim: Cxcr4 interaction with Cxcl12 is critical for the retention of neutrophils in the bone marrow under steady state.
source: Cxcr4 interaction with its ligand Cxcl12 (stromal cell-derived factor 1, SDF1) has been shown to be critical for the retention of neutrophils in the bone marrow under steady state, their release to the periphery as well as their homing back to the bone marrow when they become senescent (Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eash et al., 2010 and Martin et al., 2003

claim: Cxcr4 interaction with Cxcl12 is critical for neutrophil release to the periphery.
source: Cxcr4 interaction with its ligand Cxcl12 (stromal cell-derived factor 1, SDF1) has been shown to be critical for the retention of neutrophils in the bone marrow under steady state, their release to the periphery as well as their homing back to the bone marrow when they become senescent (Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eash et al., 2010 and Martin et al., 2003

claim: Cxcr4 interaction with Cxcl12 is critical for neutrophil homing back to the bone marrow when they become senescent.
source: Cxcr4 interaction with its ligand Cxcl12 (stromal cell-derived factor 1, SDF1) has been shown to be critical for the retention of neutrophils in the bone marrow under steady state, their release to the periphery as well as their homing back to the bone marrow when they become senescent (Eash et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eash et al., 2010 and Martin et al., 2003

claim: Cxcr4 knockout mice die perinatally due to severe developmental defects ranging from virtually absent myelopoiesis and impaired B lymphopoiesis to abnormal brain development.
source: Importantly, Cxcr4 signaling is essential, as Cxcr4 knockout mice die perinatally due to severe developmental defects ranging from virtually absent myelopoiesis and impaired B lymphopoiesis to abnormal brain development (Ma et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 1998

claim: Cxcr4 signaling delays neutrophil aging and protects from vascular damage in an ischemia reperfusion model.
source: More recently, Cxcr4 signaling was described to delay neutrophil aging and to protect from vascular damage in an ischemia reperfusion model (Adrover et al., 2019), supporting our data showing the tissue protective effects of upregulated Cxcr4 on neutrophils in sepsis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Adrover et al., 2019

claim: Tolerance was associated with a mild increase in spleen weight.
source: Tolerance was associated with a mild increase in spleen weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and total spleen cell counts, together with an expansion of B cell numbers (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by spleen weight data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Tolerance was associated with an expansion of B cell numbers in the spleen.
source: Tolerance was associated with a mild increase in spleen weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and total spleen cell counts, together with an expansion of B cell numbers (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Tolerance-induction by LPS treatment caused an expansion of transplanted B cells in spleens of Rag2-/- animals.
source: Of note, tolerance-induction by LPS treatment even caused an expansion of transplanted B cells in spleens of Rag2-/- animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Bone marrow B cell numbers increased in tolerant mice, as compared to sensitive controls.
source: In parallel, while the total number of bone marrow cells remained indistinguishable (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we found bone marrow B cell numbers increased in tolerant mice, as compared to sensitive controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Analysis of B cell subsets revealed an increase of B1 B cell numbers in spleen and bone marrow of tolerant mice.
source: Furthermore, analysis of B cell subsets revealed an increase of B1 B cell numbers (IgMhi CD23- CD43hi CD21-), a subset that also includes the B1-like innate response activator (IRA) B cells, in spleen and bone marrow (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), as well as elevated numbers of Pre-B and immature and transitional B cells (iB/tB) in the bone marrow (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Elevated numbers of Pre-B and immature and transitional B cells (iB/tB) were found in the bone marrow of tolerant mice.
source: Furthermore, analysis of B cell subsets revealed an increase of B1 B cell numbers (IgMhi CD23- CD43hi CD21-), a subset that also includes the B1-like innate response activator (IRA) B cells, in spleen and bone marrow (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), as well as elevated numbers of Pre-B and immature and transitional B cells (iB/tB) in the bone marrow (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Total numbers of follicular (FO) and marginal zone (MZ) B cells did not change upon tolerance induction.
source: In sharp contrast, total numbers of follicular (FO) and marginal zone (MZ) B cells did not change upon tolerance induction (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Elevated plasma IgM levels were found in tolerant mice prior to infection.
source: In line with this, we found elevated plasma IgM levels in tolerant mice prior to infection, which–in contrast to sensitive, control animals–returned to baseline during sepsis, indicating LPS-induced induction of IgM, and consumption of IgM during sepsis in tolerant animals (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by IgM ELISA data shown in Figure 3G

claim: IgM levels returned to baseline during sepsis in tolerant animals, indicating consumption of IgM during sepsis.
source: In line with this, we found elevated plasma IgM levels in tolerant mice prior to infection, which–in contrast to sensitive, control animals–returned to baseline during sepsis, indicating LPS-induced induction of IgM, and consumption of IgM during sepsis in tolerant animals (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by IgM ELISA data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Mice lacking soluble IgM developed less severe organ damage during sepsis.
source: Unexpectedly though, mice lacking soluble IgM developed less severe organ damage, and LPS-pretreatment still induced tissue protection during sepsis (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 3H

claim: LPS-pretreatment still induced tissue protection during sepsis in mice lacking soluble IgM.
source: Unexpectedly though, mice lacking soluble IgM developed less severe organ damage, and LPS-pretreatment still induced tissue protection during sepsis (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The B cells' tissue protective effects in tolerant mice occurred in an IgM-independent manner.
source: Taken together, tissue damage control was associated with long-term changes in the B cell compartments in the spleen and bone marrow, and the B cells' tissue protective effects in tolerant mice occurred in an IgM-independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the maintained tissue protection in IgM-deficient mice

claim: Tolerant mice exhibited lower IL-6 levels in blood and liver at 6 hours post E. coli infection compared to sensitive control mice.
source: Six hours post E. coli infection, we found tolerant wild type mice to exhibit lower IL-6 levels in blood and liver (Figure 2H), as well as lower amounts of important regulators of peritoneal leukocyte migration (Rajarathnam et al., 2019; Bianconi et al., 2018), like CXCL1 and CCL2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) when compared to sensitive control mice, a phenotype which is reminiscent of LPS-tolerance.
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2H

claim: Tolerant wild type mice exhibited lower amounts of CXCL1 and CCL2 at 6 hours post E. coli infection compared to sensitive control mice.
source: Six hours post E. coli infection, we found tolerant wild type mice to exhibit lower IL-6 levels in blood and liver (Figure 2H), as well as lower amounts of important regulators of peritoneal leukocyte migration (Rajarathnam et al., 2019; Bianconi et al., 2018), like CXCL1 and CCL2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) when compared to sensitive control mice, a phenotype which is reminiscent of LPS-tolerance.
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: Lymphocyte deficient Rag2-/- animals showed comparable reductions in IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2 in response to LPS pretreatment.
source: However, lymphocyte deficient Rag2-/- animals, in whom tissue damage control could not be improved by LPS preexposure (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), showed comparable reductions in these mediators of early inflammation in response to LPS pretreatment (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H

claim: Tissue damage control and LPS-induced disease tolerance during sepsis was induced independent of IFNAR signaling.
source: Furthermore, tissue damage control and LPS-induced disease tolerance during sepsis was induced independent of interferon-α/β receptor (IFNAR) signaling (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I) and the anti-inflammatory NF-κB subunit p50 (NF-κB1) (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), which has been shown to mediate the suppression of cytokine production during endotoxin tolerance in vitro (Fan and Cook, 2004; Ziegler-Heitbrock, 2001).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I

claim: Tissue damage control and LPS-induced disease tolerance during sepsis was induced independent of the anti-inflammatory NF-κB subunit p50 (NF-κB1).
source: Furthermore, tissue damage control and LPS-induced disease tolerance during sepsis was induced independent of interferon-α/β receptor (IFNAR) signaling (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I) and the anti-inflammatory NF-κB subunit p50 (NF-κB1) (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), which has been shown to mediate the suppression of cytokine production during endotoxin tolerance in vitro (Fan and Cook, 2004; Ziegler-Heitbrock, 2001).
evidence: Supported by liver transaminase data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J

claim: An LPS mediated modulation of early inflammation is unlikely to explain the protective effects of B cells in tolerant hosts.
source: These data suggested that in tolerant hosts, B cells contributed to tissue protection during sepsis, and that an LPS mediated modulation of early inflammation is unlikely to explain these protective effects.
evidence: Inferred from the comparable cytokine reductions in Rag2-/- mice without tissue protection

claim: LPS treatment caused substantial stress-induced granulopoiesis, peaking around day four post LPS exposure.
source: We therefore first analyzed bone marrow B cell and neutrophil dynamics after LPS challenge, and discovered substantial stress-induced granulopoiesis, peaking around day four post LPS exposure, while B cells were regulated in a reciprocal fashion as they vanished by day 4 post LPS injection, to then increase and remain elevated two weeks post LPS treatment (Figures 4B and 3C) in tolerant, as compared to sensitive animals.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B

claim: B cells vanished by day 4 post LPS injection, then increased and remained elevated two weeks post LPS treatment in tolerant mice.
source: We therefore first analyzed bone marrow B cell and neutrophil dynamics after LPS challenge, and discovered substantial stress-induced granulopoiesis, peaking around day four post LPS exposure, while B cells were regulated in a reciprocal fashion as they vanished by day 4 post LPS injection, to then increase and remain elevated two weeks post LPS treatment (Figures 4B and 3C) in tolerant, as compared to sensitive animals.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B and 3C

claim: Total and relative neutrophil numbers in the bone marrow remained slightly reduced in tolerant wild type mice.
source: At the same time total and relative neutrophil numbers in the bone marrow remained slightly reduced in tolerant wild type mice, but elevated in the absence of B cells (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Total and relative neutrophil numbers in the bone marrow were elevated in the absence of B cells.
source: At the same time total and relative neutrophil numbers in the bone marrow remained slightly reduced in tolerant wild type mice, but elevated in the absence of B cells (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: B cells promote disease tolerance by improving tissue damage control via the suppression of neutrophils' tissue-damaging properties.
source: We found that both neutrophils and B cells emerged as key regulators of tissue integrity. Enduring changes in the transcriptional profile of neutrophils include upregulated Cxcr4 expression in protected, tolerant hosts. Neutrophil Cxcr4 upregulation required the presence of B cells, suggesting that B cells promoted disease tolerance by improving tissue damage control via the suppression of neutrophils' tissue-damaging properties.
evidence: Inferred from the B cell-dependent Cxcr4 upregulation and tissue protection

claim: Therapeutic administration of a Cxcr4 agonist successfully promoted tissue damage control and prevented liver damage during sepsis.
source: Finally, therapeutic administration of a Cxcr4 agonist successfully promoted tissue damage control and prevented liver damage during sepsis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced liver damage with ATI2341 treatment

claim: Neutrophil Cxcr4 activation is a potential means to promote disease tolerance during sepsis.
source: Our findings highlight the importance of a critical B-cell/neutrophil interaction during sepsis and establish neutrophil Cxcr4 activation as a potential means to promote disease tolerance during sepsis.
evidence: Inferred from the therapeutic effects of Cxcr4 agonist administration

claim: B cells shape neutrophils' tissue-damaging properties by modulation of neutrophil Cxcr4 signaling.
source: Building on the reported interplay between these two cell populations, our data suggest that B cells shape neutrophils' tissue-damaging properties by modulation of neutrophil Cxcr4 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the B cell-dependent Cxcr4 upregulation and tissue protection

claim: Targeting Cxcr4 using a pepducin agonist protected mice from tissue damage during sepsis without affecting the bacterial load, indicating a Cxcr4-dependent disease tolerance mechanism.
source: Targeting Cxcr4 using a pepducin agonist protected mice from tissue damage during sepsis without affecting the bacterial load, indicating a Cxcr4-dependent disease tolerance mechanism.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing tissue protection without affecting bacterial load

claim: Neutrophils are the primary effector cells that drive tissue damage during sepsis.
source: Our data indicate, that neutrophils are the primary effector cells that drive tissue damage, while B cells impact tissue damage by modulating neutrophil effector functions.
evidence: Inferred from the neutrophil depletion experiments showing tissue protection

claim: B cells impact tissue damage by modulating neutrophil effector functions.
source: Our data indicate, that neutrophils are the primary effector cells that drive tissue damage, while B cells impact tissue damage by modulating neutrophil effector functions.
evidence: Inferred from the B cell-dependent effects on neutrophil Cxcr4 expression and tissue protection

claim: Mature, splenic B2 cells promote neutrophil activation by boosting type-I interferon dependent early inflammation.
source: It was demonstrated earlier that mature, splenic B2 cells promote neutrophil activation by boosting type-I interferon (IFN) dependent early inflammation, which in turn improves bacterial clearance and survival during CLP (Kelly-Scumpia et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly-Scumpia et al., 2011

claim: B1 and B1-like cells reduce neutrophil's tissue damaging effector functions, in contrast to B2 cells.
source: However, it seemed counterintuitive at first, that the absence of neutrophils or B cells, respectively, prevented tissue damage in a primary infection, while they at the same time seemed critical for tissue protection in a model of LPS-induced tolerance. We thus hypothesized that B1 and B1-like cells, in contrast to B2 cells, reduced neutrophil's tissue damaging effector functions.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the differential effects of B cell subsets

claim: sIgM deficiency goes along with a decreased abundance of B2 and an increased abundance of B1 cells.
source: As sIgM deficiency goes along with a decreased abundance of B2 and an increased abundance of B1 cells (Tsiantoulas et al., 2017) this further supported the notion of tissue damaging B2, and tissue protective B1 cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsiantoulas et al., 2017

claim: B cells, neutrophils and their precursors build up the majority of the constitutive CD45+ bone marrow cell pool.
source: In fact, B cells, neutrophils and their precursors build up the majority of the constitutive CD45+ bone marrow cell pool, where they mature while sharing the same niche (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2013

claim: Under steady state conditions in mice, only 2% of mature neutrophils circulate through the body, while the majority of cells is stored in the bone marrow.
source: Under steady state conditions in mice, only 2% of mature neutrophils circulate through the body, while the majority of cells is stored in the bone marrow from where they can be quickly released upon e.g., infection, to traffic to the periphery (Semerad et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Semerad et al., 2002

claim: Neutrophils and B cells regulate each other in a reciprocal fashion in the bone marrow.
source: It has been proposed earlier that neutrophils and B cells regulate each other in a reciprocal fashion in the bone marrow (Ueda et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ueda et al., 2005

claim: B1 B and IRA B cell-derived IgM exerts tissue protective properties and has been proposed as a possible mechanism of disease tolerance.
source: B1 B and IRA B cell-derived IgM was shown earlier to exert tissue protective properties and has been proposed as a possible mechanism of disease tolerance (Márquez-Velasco et al., 2007; Rauch et al., 2012; Weber et al., 2014; Ha et al., 2006; Murakami et al., 1994; Baumgarth, 2016; Krautz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: High plasma IgM levels positively correlate with a better outcome in human sepsis.
source: Using soluble IgM (sIgM) deficient mice (Ighm-/-), enabled us to rule out a major role for IgM in tissue damage control during sepsis, even though IgM was reported to exhibit anti-thrombotic functions in cardiovascular diseases (Binder et al., 2016) and high plasma IgM levels positively correlate with a better outcome in human sepsis (Krautz et al., 2018) and mouse models (Márquez-Velasco et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krautz et al., 2018

claim: IgM exhibits anti-thrombotic functions in cardiovascular diseases.
source: Using soluble IgM (sIgM) deficient mice (Ighm-/-), enabled us to rule out a major role for IgM in tissue damage control during sepsis, even though IgM was reported to exhibit anti-thrombotic functions in cardiovascular diseases (Binder et al., 2016) and high plasma IgM levels positively correlate with a better outcome in human sepsis (Krautz et al., 2018) and mouse models (Márquez-Velasco et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Binder et al., 2016

claim: Protective neutrophil effector functions during infection can be accompanied by severe collateral damage due to their tissue damaging properties.
source: It is well established that protective neutrophil effector functions during infection can be accompanied by severe collateral damage due to their tissue damaging properties by releasing inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β (Liu and Sun, 2019) and reactive oxygen species (Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013) or via tissue-factor mediated activation of coagulation (Maugeri and Manfredi, 2015; Østerud, 2010; Pawlinski and Mackman, 2010) and the release of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) (Kimball et al., 2016; Yipp and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies
